title: "Concepts"
guide-section: "Start Here"
---

tether borrows [jj](https://jj-vcs.dev)'s working-copy and operation-log
ideas (`new REV` to start on top of a commit, the stale-working-copy check,
an op log with `undo`). It applies them to external systems that keep their
own history. This page is the model in one sitting; the
[Overview](index.qmd#vocabulary) has the eight terms it uses.

## The working copy is the manifests

A dataset is a directory holding `tether.toml` and one manifest per object,
`.tether/objects/<key>.toml`. A manifest names the object (`kind` and
`locator`), its policy, and once committed its recorded `state` and `pin`.
Committing a dataset commits those manifests to the enclosing git or jj
repository, so history, branching, workspaces and sharing are the VCS's.
What the VCS cannot see, what tether did to the *stores*, goes in tether's
[operation log](08-configuration.qmd#operation-log).

## Commits hold pins; bookmarks hold branches

Two things are versioned, in two places.

A **dataset commit** records, for every object, an exact *state* and, where
the system can hold one, a *pin*: a native ref that keeps that state alive.
Nothing in a commit points at anything that moves: not a branch, not
"latest", not a path's current contents. That is what makes
`tether open KEY --rev C` a reproducible read months later, and what
`verify` checks.

A **bookmark** is where writes go. The working copy (`.tether/workspace.toml`,
per checkout) records which bookmark it works on and, per object, the branch
that stands for it: its *working ref*.

| Working copy is on | Each Forkable object's working ref | Fingerprinted by `commit`? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the trunk bookmark (`main`) | its upstream branch (`locator.branch`) | yes: the head is what the next commit pins |
| another bookmark, branch created | `tether.ws.<dataset>.<bookmark>` in its system | yes |
| another bookmark, branch not yet created (lazy) | pending: forked from the pin on the first writable `open` | no: until then it sits at the pin |
| no bookmark | none: read-only | no |

Objects whose system has no branches (files, Delta, DuckLake) have no
working ref: they keep their pin until a trunk `pull` reads them. The rule
is that `commit` contacts an object only if this checkout can have moved
it, the way a file you did not edit stays as the parent commit had it.
`locator.branch` is the object's *upstream*: what the trunk bookmark stands
for, what `pull` reads, and what `promote` lands on.

## State, pin, fork

For each object a backend implements three things, in increasing order of
what the system must support:

- **State**: what the object *is* now, such as an Icechunk `snapshot_id`, a
  Neon `(lsn, commit_xid, branch)`, a Delta `version`, or a file's sha256.
  Comparing states is how drift is detected without watching anything.
- **Pin**: a durable native reference to a state (an Icechunk tag, a Neon
  child branch, a git, Lance or Dolt tag), named `tether.<dataset-id>.<hash>`.
  The hash is content-addressed from `(kind, locator identity, state)`, so
  re-committing an unchanged object is a no-op. The dataset id keeps `gc`
  inside this dataset's [namespace](08-configuration.qmd#dataset-id).
- **Fork**: a writable branch created off a pin, or for `pin = "record"`
  objects off the recorded state. `tether new -b NAME` decides one per
  Forkable object, `tether.ws.<dataset-id>.<bookmark>`, created by the first
  writable `open` (or at once with `--eager`).

## Capability tiers

Backends declare capabilities, and commands degrade explicitly by tier:

- **Observed** (`FINGERPRINT`): drift detection only; `commit` records the
  state as `recoverable = false`. A local directory, an unversioned prefix.
- **Addressable** (`+ ADDRESSABLE`): the recorded state can be read back
  later with nothing to create or collect. An object in a versioned bucket,
  a Delta version, a DuckLake snapshot.
- **Pinnable** (`+ PIN`): a durable native ref can be created and deleted;
  `verify` and `gc` apply.
- **Forkable** (`+ FORK`): a writable branch can be made off a pin, so `new`
  forks and `open` returns a writable handle. Icechunk, Neon, Iceberg,
  Lance, Dolt, git.

Orthogonal flags such as `PROMOTE`, `MERGE`, `CONDITIONAL_REF` and `DIFF`
are listed per backend in [Backends](09-backends.qmd), and defined in
[Writing a Backend](11-extending.qmd#capabilities-decide-behavior).

## Handles, not data

tether is never in the data path. `open` returns a typed handle carrying the
native address (an Icechunk session on the right branch or tag, a Postgres
URL, a `DeltaTable` at a version) and steps aside. You read and write with
the system's own library.

## Store writes are plans

Most commands that write to a store compute a read-only *plan*, then
*apply* it; apply refuses (`StalePlanError`) if the world no longer matches
what the plan saw ([Plans](05-reclaiming-storage.qmd#preview-before-you-write-plans)).

## jj or tether?

Both work on the same repository, so the question comes up constantly. The
rule: **an operation gets a tether command when it has two halves, one in
the VCS and one in the stores, that must happen together.** If it only
touches files and history, use jj or git directly. tether notices what it
needs to: a moved working copy makes objects stale, and a vanished dataset
commit shows in `status` and `ops`.

The nouns map one to one. A jj *bookmark* stands for one branch per system.
jj's *snapshot on every command* is tether's **snapshot** on demand: a
concurrent fingerprint on `verify`, `status --snapshot` and `snapshot`, and
of the bookmark's branches on `commit`. A *stale working copy* is a bookmark
whose committed state changed after its branches were forked. A *detached
head* is an object registered `--at` a state, until a trunk `pull` moves it
onto the branch. A *revision with no bookmark* is a read-only working copy.

| You want to | Use | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| record the dataset's state | `tether commit` (jj: `jj commit`) | pins the bookmark's branches, writes their states into the manifests, commits, and moves the bookmark |
| start a line of work | `tether new -b NAME [REV]` (jj: `jj new -b`) | creates the bookmark *and* a branch per system named after it |
| switch to a bookmark | `tether new NAME` (jj: `jj new <bookmark>`) | moves the working copy *and* adopts that bookmark's branches |
| look at another revision without writing | `jj new REV` / `git switch` | nothing to fork; `status` says the working copy left the bookmark |
| compare two positions | `tether diff [A] [B]` (jj: `jj diff`) | an object-level manifest diff; `--content` adds native diffs |
| browse an object's own history | `tether log KEY` (jj: `jj log`) | the system's snapshots, versions or commits; the ids feed `add --at` |
| take what upstream has now | `tether pull` on `main` (jj: `jj git fetch`) | reads every upstream branch and branch-less object, and commits what moved |
| land a bookmark on `main` | `tether promote` (jj: `jj bookmark set main -r feature`) | moves each system's upstream branch, then the trunk bookmark |
| throw a bookmark away | `tether drop NAME` | drops its commits and the bookmark, then releases its pins and branches |
| reset one object to an older state | `tether restore KEY --from REV` (jj: `jj restore --from`) | the branch lives in a store; everything else stays |
| drop dataset commits | `tether abandon REV` (jj: `jj abandon`) | descendants keep their manifests, and the freed pins are planned for `gc` |
| describe, squash, rebase, split, merge | jj / git | manifests are files; run `tether gc` if commits disappeared, and `tether verify` and `tether new` after a merge |
| rename or delete a bookmark | `jj bookmark rename/delete` | `status` then says so; `gc --prune-bookmarks` releases the old branches |
| push, fetch, review | jj / git | [Sharing and CI](13-sharing-and-ci.qmd) |
| open or finish a second checkout | `jj workspace add`; `tether forget-workspace` | each checkout is its own tether workspace; forgetting one leaves the bookmark's branches |
| release what history no longer names | `tether verify`, then `tether gc` | pins and branches live in the stores |
| undo tether's last operation | `tether undo` (jj: `jj undo`) | the VCS cannot see what tether did to the stores ([Undo](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#undo)) |
| rebuild a pin or branch a manifest names | `tether repair` | manifests are the source of truth |
| publish history as SQL | `tether export` / `publish` / `import` (experimental) | a derived view of the manifests |

Two habits keep the halves aligned: `tether status` after any VCS operation
that moved the working copy or changed manifests, and `tether new` before
writing again.

### Where tether is not jj

- **Writes need a bookmark.** A store branch must exist before a write can
  land, so the bookmark is the handle both sides share. Reads (`open --rev`,
  `status`, `verify`) work on anonymous changes, as in jj.
- **`commit` moves the bookmark.** jj bookmarks do not follow commits; a
  tether bookmark must, or its branches' heads would stop matching the
  commit that names them. It happens in one jj operation, so `jj undo` takes
  both back. `commit` also starts nothing new.
- **Snapshots are on demand.** Reading a state is a network round trip, so
  `status` is local, and `status --snapshot`, `verify` and `commit` fan out.
- **The stores are remotes.** Pins are what commits reference, bookmark
  branches are local branches, `pull` is fetch, and `promote` is the push to
  `main`.

## What tether does not do

- Sit in the data path, or run between commands: there is no daemon, and
  every state is compared when a command asks.
- Cross-system atomicity: a commit records each state within a capture
  window, and point-consistency requires quiesced writers.
- Reimplement history, branching or sharing, or query across systems.
  `ops`, `undo` and `repair` cover only what tether did to the stores.
